slides.title: Modern OSH Governance and Inspection in the Energy Sector
slides.notes: Good morning, and a very warm welcome to everyone joining us from Ukraine and from our ILO and ITCILO teams. It is a pleasure to open this learning programme, Modern OSH Governance and Inspection in the Energy Sector. We are meeting online today, and next week we will have the opportunity to continue our work together in Turin. We recognise the extraordinary responsibilities carried by colleagues working to protect people and maintain essential energy services under the difficult conditions that Ukraine continues to face. Our purpose is not to offer ready-made answers from outside. It is to create a practical space where international principles, sectoral experience and Ukrainian expertise can inform each other, and where ideas can be translated into measures that work for the people and institutions represented here. Thank you for making the time to join us.

slides.title: Our two hours together
items: Welcome and opening remarks

slides.notes: Today’s programme brings together several complementary perspectives. We begin with opening remarks from Charles Crevier at the Turin Centre and Tetyana Minenko from the ILO. Casper Edmonds will then look at the energy sector as a whole, considering what is changing, how new technologies are affecting work and why occupational safety and health must remain central to a resilient sector. Changyou Zhu will help us connect these sectoral realities to international OSH principles, rights, standards and the roles of labour inspection and social partners. We will then give the floor to colleagues from Ukraine, because the lived operational experience of energy workers is indispensable to the design of this training. We will conclude with the practical aspects of our learning journey: the residential programme, study visits, eCampus, travel and accommodation, interpretation and what we need from you before departure. Questions are welcome throughout, and we will reserve time to address practical concerns together.

slides.title: Sectoral dynamics in energy
slides.sub: Decent work, OSH and the implications of new technologies and AI
topics: Transformation of energy work and skills
Protecting workers across crisis and recovery
Digital innovation, AI and the human dimension
slides.notes: Thank you for those opening reflections. We now turn to a broader sectoral perspective. Ukraine’s energy sector is addressing immediate threats to the continuity of essential services while also preparing for longer-term reconstruction and transformation. These processes raise questions not only about equipment and infrastructure, but also about the people who operate, repair and maintain these systems. New technologies can improve detection, coordination and prevention, yet their introduction must be examined alongside the organisation of work, workers’ rights, skills and the responsibilities of employers and public authorities. To help us consider these connections, I am delighted to welcome Casper Edmonds from the ILO. Casper has contributed to the ILO’s work on the energy sector in Ukraine, and his insights will help us situate OSH in the wider decent-work agenda. Casper, thank you very much. The floor is yours.

slides.title: International OSH principles and standards
slides.sub: From fundamental rights to effective prevention and enforcement
topics: Safe and healthy working environment: a fundamental principle and right at work
OSH management systems, risk assessment and prevention
Labour inspection, social partners, crisis and recovery
slides.notes: Thank you, Casper, for that important sectoral perspective. The next question is how we turn the principles we share into institutions, systems and workplace practices capable of protecting workers in exceptionally demanding circumstances. A safe and healthy working environment is a fundamental principle and right at work. International OSH instruments, including Conventions Nos. 155 and 187, provide a framework for national policy, coordinated prevention and continuous improvement. At enterprise level, the organisation of work, risk assessment, consultation and management commitment are just as important as technical protective measures. Labour inspection and meaningful engagement with workers and employers help make those commitments operational. These principles are especially relevant where work must continue in emergency, damaged or high-risk conditions. We are very pleased to welcome Changyou Zhu from the ILO to examine these dimensions and their implications for crisis and recovery. Changyou, thank you for joining us. Over to you.

people: Name and institution to be confirmed
Name and institution to be confirmed
topics: Worker realities in crisis and emergency response

slides.notes: International experience is valuable only when it is tested against the situations that workers and institutions face on the ground. This is why the voices of colleagues from Ukraine are central to our webinar and to the residential week. Across energy generation, transmission, distribution, mining and rescue services, workers have had to sustain essential activities in circumstances that demand extraordinary judgement and adaptability. We would like to hear about the risks that are most difficult to manage, practices that have helped protect workers, and priorities that would make this programme most useful. The two colleagues joining us from Ukraine will bring this operational and institutional perspective. We are especially interested in what has proved feasible under pressure, where gaps persist and what lessons could support both immediate action and longer-term recovery. Thank you very much for contributing your experience. We look forward to learning from you.

slides.title: A group with complementary expertise
items: Ministry of Energy, State Labour Service and other public authorities
Electricity transmission and distribution, OSH management and industrial safety
Mining operations and specialised mine rescue services
slides.notes: Before we introduce the Turin programme, it is worth reflecting on the expertise represented in this group. According to the current participant list, we are expecting twenty participants from Ukraine, together with one ILO colleague. Among you are colleagues from public authorities, national and regional energy operations, electricity transmission and distribution companies, enterprise occupational safety functions, mining operations and specialised mine rescue services. This mix is one of the most important strengths of the programme. Public authorities and inspectors bring the policy, regulatory and enforcement perspectives. Enterprises bring daily operational realities, including emergency maintenance, contractor arrangements and prevention systems. Mining and rescue colleagues bring direct experience of work in hazardous and rapidly changing environments. Rather than treating these as separate worlds, we want to create opportunities for learning across them. Everyone here has something significant to contribute; the programme is designed to make that expertise visible and productive.

slides.title: What brings us together
items: Protecting workers
Preventing injuries and ill-health in emergency and high-risk operations
Strengthening systems
Effective OSH management, labour inspection and cooperation
Preparing for change
Responsible use of digital tools, AI and new technologies
slides.notes: There are three connected purposes behind this training. The first is the immediate imperative to protect workers. Prevention must remain meaningful when teams are restoring power, entering damaged sites, working underground or making safety-critical decisions under severe pressure. The second purpose is to strengthen the systems that make prevention consistent and sustainable. Technical procedures matter, but so do clear responsibilities, risk assessment, labour inspection, worker participation, training and learning from incidents. The third is to prepare for change. Ukraine’s energy system will continue to evolve through reconstruction, decentralisation and new technologies. Digital reporting, remote sensing, wearables and AI may all contribute to prevention, but their introduction also requires governance, human oversight and an understanding of emerging risks. The course brings these three purposes together and asks what they mean for the decisions you make in your own institutions.

slides.notes: Our learning journey has three moments. Today’s online exchange sets the foundations. It brings international experience into dialogue with the Ukrainian context and gives us a shared understanding of the questions we will explore. The residential week takes place in Turin from 26 to 30 October. It combines technical sessions and applied work with three field visits, deliberately moving between the classroom and workplaces where occupational safety and health must be managed in practice. We then meet again online on 4 November. That final exchange will include strategic foresight on emerging OSH risks and a closing discussion focused on reflection and practical next steps. The aim is not to treat the residential course as an isolated event, but to encourage continued application of lessons in the institutions and workplaces represented here. The exact time-zone reference for the 4 November webinar will be reconfirmed in the course communications.

slides.title: What we want to take home
items: Sharper identification and assessment of high-priority energy-sector OSH risks
Stronger emergency protocols, preventive controls and PPE choices
Practical ways to improve inspection, worker participation and OSH management
Responsible applications of digital tools and AI for prevention
Concrete priorities for institutional and workplace follow-up
slides.notes: By the end of the programme, we want you to have more than a collection of presentations. You should have a stronger basis for identifying the most urgent occupational risks in your area of responsibility and for assessing whether existing controls are sufficient. We will look closely at emergency repair procedures, preparedness, personal protective equipment and decision-making in high-risk environments. We will examine how management systems, labour inspection and worker participation can reinforce each other. We will also consider how digital technology and AI can help identify hazards, improve reporting and support timely decisions without diminishing human responsibility for safety. Most importantly, we will encourage you to identify realistic priorities for follow-up. These may differ between ministries, inspection bodies, electricity operators and mine rescue services. That diversity is expected and valuable. The common measure of success is whether the learning can contribute to safer work.

slides.title: The residential week at a glance
days: IREN: OSH in an energy company
slides.notes: Here is the overall progression of the week. We begin on Monday with the realities of protecting energy workers in crisis and recovery and work through occupational safety and health management systems, risk assessment and decision-making during emergency repairs. Tuesday turns to innovation for prevention, including digital tools and AI, alongside PPE, preparedness and the role of labour inspection. We also prepare an observation framework for the study visits. Wednesday takes us to IREN, where we will consider prevention in an energy company or utility environment. Thursday focuses on Sogin and the particular demands of managing high-risk energy operations. On Friday we will visit Imerys Talc Italy for an underground mining perspective. Each of the visits has a different emphasis, but they are designed to inform a common question: what can be adapted to strengthen protection of energy-sector workers in Ukraine? Detailed session titles and contributors are provided on the following agenda slides.

slides.title: Three study visits, three perspectives
sites: Safety management in utility operations, prevention and worker participation
Complex operational risks, protective systems and safety oversight
Mining hazards, controls, emergency arrangements and safety culture
slides.notes: These visits are a particularly important part of the learning design. They are not organised as general tours. Each site offers a different perspective on how high-risk work can be planned, supervised and carried out safely. At IREN, we will focus on the management of occupational safety and health in an energy company or utility environment: preventive systems, responsibilities, monitoring and worker involvement. At Sogin, our attention will turn to the requirements of high-risk energy operations and the organisational and technical arrangements needed to manage complex hazards. At Imerys Talc Italy, we will focus on underground mining conditions, critical risks, preventive engineering, preparedness and safety culture. We encourage you to compare these perspectives rather than look for a single model to copy. The value of the visits will lie in identifying which principles and practices can be adapted responsibly to different Ukrainian energy and mining workplaces.

items: Governance

Risk controls

Preparedness

Worker voice

Learning
How are incidents, near misses and inspections translated into change?
slides.notes: Our goal during each visit is to look beyond the visible equipment and understand the prevention system around it. We will ask who holds responsibility for occupational safety and health, how managers and workers coordinate, and where inspectors and external actors fit in. We will pay attention to the way risks are identified before tasks begin, how controls are selected and checked, and how the organisation knows whether its preventive measures are working. We will also look at preparedness: what happens when normal conditions change, when equipment fails or when a worker needs to be evacuated or rescued? Worker participation matters just as much as procedures and engineering. What opportunities do workers have to raise concerns, challenge unsafe decisions or report near misses without fear? Finally, we will ask how lessons from incidents, observations and inspections feed back into improvements. We will use a common set of questions so that each of you can compare the three sites and relate their practices to your own working environment.

slides.notes: The residential week is designed to be active, collaborative and directly connected to professional practice. There will be technical inputs from ILO specialists and external experts, but we do not intend to spend the entire week listening to lectures. Group work will provide opportunities to examine concrete issues such as risk assessment, protective measures, emergency repair procedures, inspection and digital innovation. The study visits will allow us to observe how organisations address prevention in real operational settings. Most importantly, after each visit we will create space to discuss what participants have noticed and how those observations might be used in Ukraine. Not every measure will be transferable, and we will treat that question critically. The Information Note specifies an ITCILO Certificate of Participation for those who meet the mandatory activity requirements and attend at least eighty per cent of the sessions. We therefore encourage active participation throughout the week.

slides.title: Experts and contributors across the week
slides.notes: Throughout the programme, participants will work with a range of ILO, ITCILO and external specialists whose contributions cover complementary dimensions of occupational safety and health. Tetyana Minenko, Casper Edmonds, Changyou Zhu and Ahmet Dukunlu will help connect the Ukrainian context, sectoral work, international principles and labour inspection. Riccardo Melandri will contribute technical expertise on OSH management systems, risk assessment and emergency operational decisions. Claudio Galbiati will focus on prevention, new technologies, artificial intelligence and protective measures. Sara Bonatto will bring specialist experience of mining and underground safety, while Camila Pereira Rego Meireles will contribute to the discussion of modern and inclusive energy work. Colleagues from the State Labour Service of Ukraine are included in the programme, and ILO OSHE is expected to contribute to the follow-up session on strategic foresight. The intention is to make these perspectives interact with one another and, above all, with your own experience.
